When dealing with data ordering in modern Java, developers frequently choose between invoking the intermediate sorted() method on a Stream and sorting a collection in place using methods like Collections.sort() or List.sort(). While both mechanisms ultimately rearrange elements according to a natural or custom Comparator, their underlying execution semantics, memory footprints, and architectural placement diverge drastically. In-place sorting mutates the existing data structure directly, prioritizing minimal heap allocation and localized state modification. Conversely, sorted() in streams operates within the functional, declarative paradigm introduced in Java 8, treating data flows as immutable transformations. It acts as a stateful intermediate operation, which fundamentally changes how the JVM pipeline processes elements from source to sink.

To understand the deep technical divergence, one must examine how streams handle data. A stream pipeline consists of a source, zero or more intermediate operations, and a terminal operation. Operations are categorized as stateless (like map or filter, which process elements independently) or stateful (like sorted or distinct). When sorted() is invoked on a stream, it cannot emit the first downstream element until it has consumed, buffered, and evaluated every single upstream element. This implies that lazy evaluation is temporarily suspended for the sorting phase. The stream machinery must accumulate references to all incoming elements into an internal collection—typically an array—sort that array using a dual-pivot Quicksort or TimSort algorithm, and then emit the sorted elements sequentially to the next stage in the pipeline. This introduces significant memory overhead and synchronization barriers, contrasting sharply with in-place collection sorting which directly reorganizes pointers within an existing ArrayList or LinkedList instance.

rows: Immutable pipeline; creates a new logical sequence without mutating the source collection.
Mutable; directly reorganizes element references inside the target collection.
Higher; requires buffering all elements in memory to perform the sorting algorithm before downstream emission.
Lower; sorts the existing underlying array or node pointers without allocating a secondary staging buffer.
Stateful intermediate stream operation; blocks downstream execution until the entire upstream barrier is cleared.
Eager algorithmic execution; immediately reorganizes the data structure upon invocation.
Seamlessly integrates into declarative chains (e.g., filter().sorted().map()).
Requires breaking the fluent stream flow; must be performed before stream creation or via collection mutations.

items: Stateful Operation Barrier: sorted() introduces a execution barrier in the Stream pipeline. The JVM cannot optimize this with short-circuiting or parallel chunking without first establishing total order, which forces a full synchronization point across the data set.

Algorithm Implementation: Both mechanisms ultimately delegate to robust sorting algorithms under the hood—such as TimSort for objects and dual-pivot Quicksort for primitives—ensuring $O(N \log N)$ average time complexity.

Garbage Collection Impact: Because stream sorted() often allocates internal arrays to hold intermediate references before emitting them, heavy usage in high-throughput loops can elevate minor collection pressure on the JVM Eden space compared to mutating an existing reusable list.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap occurs when developers attempt to use sorted() on an infinite or extremely large lazy stream (such as a database cursor or network socket stream) without a preceding limit() or dropWhile(). Because sorted() must buffer all elements into memory to complete the sort, executing it on an unbounded stream will inevitably trigger an OutOfMemoryError (java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space). Always apply slicing operations to bound your data size before invoking stateful intermediate operations like sorted().
